Explainer

What is the UN Security Council?

The Security Council is the organ of the United Nations with primary responsibility for international peace and security. Under Article 25 of the UN Charter, all member states agree to carry out its decisions.

Members

Fifteen members: five permanent (China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States) and ten elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms. The Council had eleven members until the Charter amendment of 1965 enlarged it. The presidency rotates every month. Current members and voting records.

How it decides

A resolution needs nine votes in favour and no veto from a permanent member. What veto power is, and every veto since 1946.

What it can do

Under Chapter VI of the Charter the Council recommends ways to settle disputes peacefully. Under Chapter VII, once it determines a "threat to the peace, breach of the peace, or act of aggression" (Article 39), it can impose binding measures: sanctions, arms embargoes, peace operations, tribunals, and the use of force by member states. How the Council used those three words and how Chapter VII became routine.

In numbers

Security Council Record is an independent record of every resolution, vote and veto of the United Nations Security Council since 1946. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by the United Nations. For official documents, use the Security Council website and the UN Digital Library.
